strengths: The paper addresses a useful NLP problem: forecasting pretraining loss from an early training prefix to support hyperparameter selection directly on the target model.

The empirical investigation is substantial. It includes models up to 6.7B parameters, ID and OOD evaluation, and additional GPT-NeoX and MoE fitting experiments. The larger-model forecasting results provide meaningful evidence beyond retrospective curve fitting and outperform the reported baselines.

The data-mixture application provides encouraging practical evidence: the selected mixtures reduce perplexity in all four model/dataset settings and improve 12 of 14 downstream task comparisons. Equations, configuration tables, package versions, and pseudocode also provide useful methodological detail.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate the benefit of token-position decomposition. The proposed predictor uses piecewise functions and explicit learning-rate schedule information, whereas the baselines use simple scalar power, logarithmic, or reciprocal functions. After the separation point, Eqs. (8) and (10) reduce aggregate loss to a constant plus a2(N). A scalar predictor using the same piecewise forms and schedule information is therefore an essential control. The directly relevant schedule-aware predictor of Luo et al. (2025), already cited by the manuscript, should also be compared.

The functional-form comparisons contain unresolved numerical inconsistencies. Section 2.3 reports power-law R² below 0.75 for over 95% of checkpoints, while Table 9 reports R² above 0.95 for 67% of the 58M checkpoints. Table 9 also gives strongly negative in-sample R² for exponential fits, suggesting optimization problems given the free-offset formulation. These results need reconciliation and documented fitting diagnostics.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful configuration tables. The evaluation interval, nonlinear-fit initialization and constraints, outlier-removal thresholds, and actual mixture candidates and selected weights are unspecified. Algorithm 1, lines 29–30, applies the calibration under the opposite separation-point condition from Section 2.4. The manuscript supplies no implementation or raw-loss-trace link that would resolve these ambiguities.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence does not establish reliable ranking at the operational prediction horizon. Selection uses 10B of 400B tokens, or 2.5%, whereas forecasting experiments evaluate 10–40% prefixes. Candidate-level predictions and final ranking accuracy at 2.5% are not reported. Perplexity improvements are approximately 0.7–1.3%, and averaging five adjacent checkpoints does not quantify independent-run uncertainty. Ranking reliability, uncertainty, and total search cost need clearer evaluation.

The theoretical interpretations exceed what is established. Equation (17) follows from manually holding a0 and a1 constant; it is not an independent theoretical explanation of uniform learning progress. Figure 11 and three weighting variants provide limited empirical support, but do not establish that position weighting is generally unnecessary. Appendix C also incorrectly excludes exponential behavior on asymptotic grounds: an exponential with a positive offset can approach a nonzero loss floor.

The generic-law framing is broader than the demonstrated forecasting scope. Experiments primarily use the Pile and cosine schedules; the linear-schedule and additional-architecture results mainly establish retrospective fit quality. Narrowing these claims would help, but the controlled-comparison, reporting, and reproducibility issues still require revision before a positive Findings recommendation.
